patient.chief_complaint: Witnessed brief shaking then prolonged confusion and abnormal movements for 50 minutes, fever present
patient.history_present_illness: A 66-year-old Hispanic male retired mechanic was brought to the emergency department by his son, who witnessed a brief tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. The patient has no known history of epilepsy. His son reports that over the past 2 weeks, his father had been having progressive memory difficulty, confusion, and behavioral changes — he kept repeating questions, got lost driving to a familiar gas station, and had been sleeping 14-16 hours per day. He had also complained of intermittent headaches. No fever at home was noted initially. After the brief shaking stopped, the patient did not return to baseline. Instead, over the following 20 minutes, the son noticed his father making repetitive unusual hand and finger movements — rubbing his thumb and index finger together continuously — and intermittently smacking his lips. EMS temperature was 38.2°C. He has a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia but no neurological conditions. He takes metformin and lisinopril. Recently, his primary care physician started him on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for a urinary tract infection 12 days ago. He also takes over-the-counter cetirizine for seasonal allergies. No known immunosuppression. Son denies alcohol use, illicit drugs, or recent travel outside the state. No sick contacts. No known tuberculosis exposure. Family history: father had Alzheimer's dementia at 78. Wife died of breast cancer. Son and daughter healthy.

results.title: Herpes simplex encephalitis: diagnosis and treatment update
results.key_finding: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for 14-21 days is the established treatment duration for herpes simplex encephalitis. Neurological sequelae including memory impairment and post-encephalitic epilepsy are reported in 30-40% of patients despite antiviral therapy. Non-convulsive seizure activity has been reported in HSV encephalitis and EEG monitoring is used for detection. Adjunctive corticosteroids remain of unproven benefit and are not standard of care.

output.summary: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1 predominantly in adults) is treated with IV acyclovir for 14-21 days; CSF HSV PCR is the diagnostic standard with sensitivity of 96-98% when performed within 2-10 days of symptom onset. Non-convulsive seizures and status epilepticus have been reported in the acute phase; antiseizure medications are used concurrently with antivirals for seizure management. Crystallization nephropathy is a recognized complication of IV acyclovir; adequate hydration reduces this risk. Post-encephalitic epilepsy and memory impairment are reported as sequelae in a significant proportion of survivors.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
DaTscan / dopamine transporter imaging has no role in SE; no parkinsonism question relevant to acute management.

critical_actions: Start empiric IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h IMMEDIATELY once HSV is suspected — do not wait for PCR
Adequate IV fluids during acyclovir to prevent crystal nephropathy
Load IV levetiracetam as ESETT second-line
Continuous EEG to monitor NCSE response
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric acyclovir while waiting for HSV PCR — early treatment dramatically improves outcomes
Do NOT perform LP without prior CT exclusion of mass effect
Do NOT use phenytoin in the setting of fever + dehydration without close cardiac monitoring
key_reasoning_points: HSV encephalitis classically involves the unilateral temporal lobe with mesial temporal FLAIR / DWI signal
Empiric acyclovir must start immediately whenever HSV is on the differential — delays cost lives
Post-HSV NMDAR encephalitis can emerge during recovery; repeat autoimmune panel if clinical deterioration after HSV treatment
NCSE accompanies HSV encephalitis in many patients and requires both antiviral and AED treatment
